en: The Treasury of Dohās by Kāṇhapāda. Om, homage to the Holder of the Vajra! I bear the pride of the world; I am proficient in the ultimate truth.
If even one among ten million were to become absorbed in the stainless [state], [then] pride prevails in the world.
(1) The meaning of this is as follows:
[People] maintain arrogance in the world.

"Who is this one who is 'I am all,' proficient in the ultimate truth?"—and this [claim] may indeed be appropriate as long as it is possible. Therefore, if even a single person among millions of yogis becomes "merged in the stainless" (*nirañjanalīna*), then he is such a one. That which is "stainless" (*nirañjana*) is the Sahaja-kāya, so called because the "stains"—the afflictions such as passion and hatred—have departed from it. Merged in that, with his mind submerged therein, is the Lord of Yogins; and the sense is that he is like me.
Scholars carry the pride of their learning in the Āgamas, Vedas, and Purāṇas;
like bees driven out by a ripe fruit of fortune, they wander about in falsehood.
2. The meaning is as follows:
The learned carry the conceit of having realized the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) through knowledge derived from external scriptures and the like.

Being in such a state, what do they do and where? He says: just as bees (*ali*) hover over ripe *śrīphala* fruits, being drawn by the scent of the exterior, so too, because their vision is obstructed by the apparent reality of external knowledge such as that found in scriptures, they do not contemplate the nectar-like essence of the profound reality (*tattva*). This is the meaning.
And so it has been said by the Great Sage in the *Caturdevīparipṛcchā-mahāyogatantra*, within the eighty-four thousand sections of the Dharma:
"Those who do not indeed know reality—all of them are truly without fruit. (149)
He stated this proof:
"The Siddha, adorned with eloquence, has been seen by me in my own body as naturally blissful, like a lotus unstirred [by the wind]. (3)
This is the meaning:
the bodhicitta, which is the nature of conventional vibration, is the semen adorned with the female essence (rajas); it is embraced by the mind-vajra.
To the question "What is the mind-vajra?", he says: the *pokkhara* is the lotus-tree to be described hereafter; its seed exists by way of the nature of bliss.
He asks, "Where is that very pure mind-vajra seen? and replies:
"By the word 'own' (*nija*), one's own body is meant as being presided over by gnosis; that very [body] is understood as being seen through the thread of the lake.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
Space, water, nectar, fire, and the root—these are abandoned;
the Avadhūtī is cultivated, and even the sound "Haṃ" at the root and the stalk perish.
4. This is the meaning.

Because its nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the sky is water and Amitābha is the deity of the joy of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). Having made the mud the root and the stalk, the primary cause is meditated upon. Producing that very mind of awakening through the sequence of stalk, leaf, cluster, and so forth, he says this for that purpose:
she is called *avadhūtī* because she shakes off (*dhunoti*) afflictions and other evils with ease (*avahelayā*), that is, effortlessly (*anābhogena*).

The syllable *haṃ*—meaning "the root and stalk made by the *avadhūtī*"—refers to the cause of the root and stalk being fashioned by that *avadhūtī*. Furthermore, by means of the syllable *haṃ*, which will be described as having the form of nectar (*makaranda*), the Unstruck (*anāhata*) arises as Vajradhara in the form of the syllables of Vajrānaṅga; this is the meaning. (150) Now, one might ask: what are those stalks, lotus fibers, and petals that have been made into the root by the *avadhūtī*? To this he says:
The *lalanā* and *rasanā* are the two banks adorned with the sun and moon;
at their meeting point, where four channels converge, stands the abode of great bliss.
(5) The meaning is as follows:
In the left nostril, Lalanā resides as the nature of the moon of wisdom;
in the right nostril, Rasanā resides as the nature of the sun of skillful means;
the two [channels] are situated as neuter.
On the two sides, the left and the right, there are two tufts.
And so it is said in the *Hevajra*:
"Lalanā exists by nature as wisdom (*prajñā*), while Rasanā is established as method (*upāya*)."
"The *avadhūtī* is in the middle region, devoid of the grasped and the grasper.
Thus, the "grasped" is the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the "grasper" is the cognition (*jñāna*); it is devoid of these two.
The intended meaning there is that it is non-different from the dyad.

The meaning is that because there is no error regarding the relationship between the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the knowledge itself (*jñāna*), which stand in the relation of produced and producer, their attainment of existence is excluded.

The four leaves exist in the form of the four voids—namely, the Void, the Exceeding Void, the Great Void, and the Universal Void—and they are situated upon four lotus stalks in the form of the four [elements] and so forth. Where? He says: "The abode of great bliss" (*mahāsukhavāsa*) refers to the *uṣṇīṣa* lotus, wherein resides the abode of the universal void; it is called the "Holder of the Net" (*jāladharā*), whose nature is the *ḍākinījāla*, and its meaning is the peak of Mount Meru.

Having thus taken the seed, the hero of sexual union (suratavīra) smells the nectar of the blossomed lotus in the form of a bee; for he is a "hero" because he has subdued passion through the yoga of the mind-as-vajra and wisdom as means, which takes the form of uninterrupted great passion. 6.
The meaning is that the Vajra experiences the *makaranda*— the nectar of the supreme bliss of sexual union— which is imperishable (*acyuta*), great passion, and blissful consciousness.
It is not that [the senses] themselves, having become objects, smell the fruit produced through the beginningless sequence.
How is this seen in another scripture?
Thus it is said in the Śrī Hevajra:
"He himself is the creator, he himself is the destroyer, he himself is the king, he himself is the lord."
"Self-remover" means that he himself is of the nature of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
"Self-lord" means he is endowed with sovereignty over all.
Like a jewel of universal form, his very nature consists of manifestation, vibration, and withdrawal.
Just as the five great elements come together in union, earth, water, fire, wind, and space are joined together. 7.
This is the meaning.

Having taken the seed consisting of the five great elements—the pentad of earth, water, fire, wind, and space—and through their conjunction by way of the union of the *volaka* and *kakkola*, he explains that very same [process]: from hardness, earth is solid;
from fluidity, water; from the friction of heat, the consuming fire arises; from space, the wind;
and from the nature of bliss, space.
The meaning is that the body is a complete assembly of the five elements (*bhūta*). As it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
"Why is the aggregate (*skandha*) elemental?"
The Blessed One said: Through the union of the *volaka* and *kakkola*, from the contact of that which has the nature of hardness,
earth is produced therein.
From the appearance of the melting of bodhicitta, the earth element arises;
from friction, fire is born; and from movement, wind is proclaimed. Bliss is the space element, which is situated all around these five.
This is the meaning:
"therein" means that the earth element arises within the innate (*sahaja*).
The intention is that *bola* is the *vajra* and *kakkola* is the *padma*; thus, it is through the union of the *vajra* and the *padma*.
Therein, the innate *bodhicitta* arises; semen is produced. Because it has the nature of the moon (*candra*), there is the "origination" (*sambhava*) or production of water.
From friction, fire (*tejas*) is born.
Through the friction of the vajra and the lotus, the fire element (tejodhātu) arises.
From space, wind is proclaimed; because its nature is movement, it is proclaimed as the wind element (vāyudhātu).
Bliss is the space element (ākāśadhātu), because its nature is bliss.
In this void, which is filled with the five [senses] and the pleasant fragrance of the wind from the sky, all the gods and asuras cry out, "This is it! This is that void! (8).
The meaning is as follows:
The sky is space (*ākāśa*) and the wind is air (*samīraṇa*); [the body] is filled with these five great elements (*mahābhūta*) as a pleasant dwelling and a place of comfort for both.
These five are the cause of the birth of all beings, including humans, gods, and demons. To explain what those gods and demons are like, he says:
Because of being devoid of this knowledge, one is addressed with the word "fool" (*mūrkha*).
This very pentad of elements, due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), is the Void, the waveless Fourth, which is the form of the Innate (*sahaja*)—this is the meaning. And so it is said:
having encountered salt water in one place, someone concludes that the entire ocean of milk is likewise [of that same nature].
Having understood that existence has a single nature, one likewise delimits the entire triple world as being a mere part [of that nature].
Such is another mode:
the sense organ of earth is the nose, and its object is odor.
Odor exists only in earth and nowhere else.
The sense organ of water is the tongue; its object is taste, and it perceives taste alone by necessity.
The sense organ of fire is the eye; its object is form.
The sense organ of air is the skin; its object is touch, specifically the touch of the female and male organs and so forth.
The sense organ of space is the ear; its object is sound, for it perceives sound alone and nothing else by necessity. Clarifying this very point, he says: (153)
"O Earth, Water, Fire, Wind, and Space, take measure by means of the increase of the poison of the maṇḍala-cakra! 9.

This very pentad of elements is the object; the cognition that arises therein from the union of the vajra and the lotus—that pleasant mental state is "object-cognition" (*viṣayabuddhi*). Taking hold of that [cognition] through instruction such as mine, [one perceives] earth, water, fire, wind, and space...
Practice until you reach the limit.
To explain what that state is like, he says:
"Free from waves, even, of its innate nature, and devoid of all impurities."
"In the state devoid of sin and merit, there is no reproach; this is clearly explained.
(10) The meaning is as follows:

due to the absence of waves, it is waveless, equal, the state of *nirvāṇa*, the innate form (*sahajarūpa*), free from all impurities, and devoid of passions and other sins; that is to say, it is completely abandoned [by them]. And so it has been stated by the venerable Ādibuddha:
There is no sin greater than passion, nor is there any merit greater than bliss;
therefore, O King, one should always fix the mind upon unchanging bliss (*akṣarasukha*).
Consequently, by this means, the three realms should be understood as having the nature of the waveless innate (*sahaja*), because they are composed of the five great elements.
And so it is said in the Śrī Hevajra:
"Bliss is black, bliss is yellow, bliss is red, bliss is white;
bliss is blue, bliss is black, and bliss is all that is moving and unmoving."

Thus, in such a state, although it is designated as "great bliss" (*mahāsukha*), it is an abiding free from suffering; therein, neither "sin"—which is the suffering of passion and so forth—nor "merit"—which is the pleasure of passion—exists even in the slightest degree.
And so it is said in the *Śrī Sampuṭa*:
"Having abandoned both passion and dispassion, he remains once again."
And this was clearly stated by Kṛṣṇācārya; the meaning is that it was not stated by others.
And this knowledge is for the purpose of external application by those whose minds are turned outward.

Showing that what has arisen is black, dark, variegated, and born of painful hardship, he says: "O rogue! The young woman, adorned with peacock feathers, has entered the empty space; in the midst of that empty space, O wretch, I have seen nothing at all. (11)
This is the meaning:

having arranged the wheel of forms through the emptiness of all external phenomena that have gone forth, and having mentally entered even the end of passion within the non-empty body by means of imagined yoga, at that time, O fool, nothing whatsoever—a reality—was seen or known in the middle of these two, namely emptiness and non-emptiness, which constitute the root. This is the sense.

If it were thus that there is no reality whatsoever, he says: "The innate alone is the supreme; it exists there clearly, yet who truly knows it? Though one reads and hears many scriptures and traditions, O fool, one knows nothing at all. (12)
This is the meaning: there exists one supreme reality that is innate (*sahaja*). And that the Supreme Kṛṣṇavajra alone knows.

Although he reads and teaches various scriptures such as logic (*tarka*) and so forth, and listens to and causes others to listen to the manifold Āgamas such as the Kriyā and Caryā tantras, he understands nothing at all, because he is turned away from the secrets of the unsurpassed Mantra system, such as the Vajrayāna.
Furthermore, the meaning is that only one like me knows the supreme.
"I do not go, nor does he come;
free from duality, he remains motionless. (155)
Kāṇha says: the mind does not burst open by any means;
it remains as motionless as the wind in the house of a housewife.
(13) It does not go downward because of the restraint of the apāna-vāyu; it does not go upward because of the restraint of the prāṇa-vāyu.

It is devoid of and abandoned by the two, the upward and downward breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*); having expelled his *bodhicitta* in such a manner, he remains. Demonstrating that very point, Kṛṣṇācārya says: "O mind, *bodhicitta* does not manifest in any way; it does not take root"—this is the meaning.
To clarify where such a bodhicitta resides, he says:
"In the deep, excellent mountain ravines and caves, the entire world collapses;
even the pure waters dry up if the fire of time (kālāgni) enters. (14)
This is the meaning:
"vara" means the most excellent mountain, Meru, which has the form of a skeleton.
And likewise, in the *Śrīsampuṭa*:
The Bhairava wind, shaped like a bow, resides at the soles of the feet;
it likewise resides in the region of the hips as the upholder of the triangle.
Varuṇa, whose form is circular, resides in the three-petaled [lotus].

"In the heart, the earth is indeed square on all sides; likewise, Sumeru, the king of mountains, is in the form of the spinal column. Regarding that, he speaks of what exists within its cave—the hollow—which is profound because it is beyond the range of the five [senses]: "Within that cave, O Goddess, there is a supreme abode, A palace of jewels, adorned with various gems. There, O Goddess, resides the Lord of the World, The Supreme Being, the Great Lord, the Self-born. || 105-106 || [He asks: "What is it that exists there? [The text] says: "The Lord of the World, the Supreme Being, the Self-born, The Great Lord, the Unmanifest, the Unstruck (Anāhata), The Unchanging, the Stainless, the One who is without beginning or end, The Eternal, the Blissful, the One who is without decay. || 107 || [He asks: "How does one perceive Him? [The text] says: "One perceives Him through the power of yoga, By means of the supreme, stainless concentration. Having perceived Him, one attains liberation, Beyond the reach of birth and death. || 108 || [He asks: "By what means does one attain Him? [The text] says: "By means of the supreme, stainless yoga, Through the grace of the Guru and the scripture. One who is devoted to the practice of the mantra, Attains the state of the Supreme Lord. || 109 || [He asks: "What is the nature of that state? [The text] says: "That state is free from all conceptualization, Beyond the reach of speech and mind. It is the supreme bliss, the ultimate reality, The very essence of the universe. || 110 || [He asks: "How does one abide in that state? [The text] says: "Abiding in that state, one is liberated, Free from all bondage and suffering. One becomes the Lord of the Universe, Equal to the Supreme Lord Himself. || 111 || [He asks: "Is there any distinction between the Guru and the disciple in this regard? [The text] says: "There is no distinction between the Guru and the disciple, For both are of the same nature as the Supreme Lord. Through the grace of the Guru, the disciple attains, The state of the Supreme Lord, without doubt. || 112 || [He asks: "What is the fruit of this knowledge? [The text] says: "The fruit of this knowledge is liberation, The attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord. One who knows this, O Goddess, Is freed from the cycle of birth and death. || 113 || [He asks: "How should one worship Him? [The text] says: "One should worship Him with devotion, Offering flowers, incense, and lamps. With a pure mind and a focused heart, One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord. || 114 || [He asks: "What is the result of such worship? [The text] says: "By worshipping Him with devotion, One attains all desires and powers. One becomes invincible to all enemies, And is honored by gods and men. || 115 || [He asks: "Is there any danger in this practice? [The text] says: "There is no danger in this practice, Provided one follows the instructions of the Guru. One who acts contrary to the teachings, Falls into the abyss of hell. || 116 || [He asks: "What is the final destination of such a person? [The text] says: "The final destination of such a person, Is the realm of the Supreme Lord. There, they enjoy eternal bliss, Free from all suffering and fear. || 117 || [He asks: "Is there any difference between this path and other paths? [The text] says: "There is no difference between this path and others, For all paths lead to the same goal. But this path is the most direct, The swiftest way to liberation. || 118 || [He asks: "How should one maintain this practice? [The text] says: "One should maintain this practice constantly, Without interruption or distraction. One should remain mindful at all times, Remembering the Supreme Lord in the heart. || 119 || [He asks: "What is the sign of success in this practice? [The text] says: "The sign of success in this practice, Is the vision of the Supreme Lord. One sees Him clearly, without doubt, And attains the state of eternal bliss. || 120 || [He asks: "Is there any need for external rituals? [The text] says: "There is no need for external rituals, If one possesses inner purity and devotion. The true ritual is the purification of the mind, The renunciation of all worldly attachments. || 121 || [He asks: "What is the ultimate truth of this teaching? [The text] says: "The ultimate truth of this teaching, Is the realization of the non-dual nature. All phenomena are empty and devoid of self, Yet manifest as the play of the Supreme Lord. || 122 || [He asks: "How does one express this truth? [The text] says: "One expresses this truth through silence, Beyond words and concepts. It is the ineffable, the inconceivable, The very essence of the universe. || 123 || [He asks: "Is there any possibility of error in this teaching? [The text] says: "There is no possibility of error in this teaching, For it is the word of the Supreme Lord Himself. One who doubts this teaching, Falls into the darkness of ignorance. || 124 || [He asks: "What is the role of the Guru in this process? [The text] says: "The role of the Guru is paramount, For without the Guru's grace, one cannot attain liberation. The Guru is the embodiment of the Supreme Lord, The guide on the path to enlightenment. || 125 || [He asks: "How should one honor the Guru? [The text] says: "One should honor the Guru with reverence, Offering service and devotion. The Guru is the bridge to the divine, The source of all blessings and wisdom. || 126 || [He asks: "Is there any limit to the Guru's power? [The text] says: "There is no limit to the Guru's power, For the Guru is the master of all mysteries. Through the Guru's power, one transcends, All obstacles and limitations. || 127 || [He asks: "What is the final instruction? [The text] says: "The final instruction is this: Remain in the state of equanimity, Free from attachment and aversion. This is the path to liberation, The way to the Supreme Lord. || 128 || [He asks: "Is there any need for further explanation? [The text] says: "There is no need for further explanation, For the truth has been revealed in its entirety. One who understands this, Has attained the highest goal. || 129 || [He asks: "What is the nature of the Supreme Lord? [The text] says: "The nature of the Supreme Lord, Is beyond description and definition. He is the source of all existence, The unmanifest, the eternal. || 130 || [He asks: "How does one realize His nature? [The text] says: "One realizes His nature through meditation, By dissolving the mind in the heart. When the mind is stilled, one sees, The light of the Supreme Lord. || 131 || [He asks: "Is there any distinction between the waking and dreaming states? [The text] says: "There is no distinction between the waking and dreaming states, For both are manifestations of the mind. When the mind is purified, one sees, The unity of all experiences. || 132 || [He asks: "What is the significance of the heart? [The text] says: "The significance of the heart is great, For it is the seat of consciousness. In the heart, one finds the source, Of all thoughts and perceptions. || 133 || [He asks: "Is there any need for external symbols? [The text] says: "There is no need for external symbols, If one possesses inner awareness. The true symbol is the realization, Of the non-dual nature of reality. || 134 || [He asks: "What is the ultimate goal? [The text] says: "The ultimate goal is liberation, The attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord. One who reaches this goal, Is freed from the cycle of birth and death. || 135 || [He asks: "Is there any possibility of regression? [The text] says: "There is no possibility of regression, Once one has attained the
In that regard, the entire world arises and becomes stabilized within the element of selflessness (*nairātmyadhātu*).
To the question "What happens by this?", he says:

the stainless *bodhicitta*, which is of the nature of bliss through cessation, having the form of conventional semen in the water, reaches a state of purity and equality; it undergoes drying up and falls downward. Thus he speaks.
And so it is said in the *Śukrasiddhi*:
"When the bodhicitta, the treasury of all accomplishments, has fallen, and when the consciousness of the aggregates has fainted, how can there be blameless accomplishment? (156)
Regarding the state of the emission of the fire of time (*kālāgni-ścuti*), which begins at the moment of entering the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pratipad*): how is this so?
He says that one experiences the bliss of great passion (*mahārāga*) within the Imperishable (*acyuta*):
"This is that upward-moving form; O Supporter of the Earth, it finds no passage through the even or uneven [channels]."
Kāṇha says: "Difficult to perceive, difficult to traverse—who can comprehend this in the mind?
(15). The meaning is this:
this very novice yogin, by means of the painful restraint of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, through the total immobility of the mind, does not move; indeed, the moon does not waver.
Thus, the previously mentioned Meru is "even and uneven" there due to the entry and exit of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths; likewise, it does not reach the summit of the Northern Meru.

For this very reason, Kṛṣṇavajra says: "Because it is unperceived by the gods, uncommon to the Śrāvakas and others, and beyond the range of [ordinary] yogins, who in their minds contemplates that supreme reality which is difficult to fathom? He who knows it—that jewel of the mind, which touches the innate (*sahaja*) day and night."
He alone knows the true course of the Dharma; what else could he possibly understand while speaking?

(16) He who perceives the jewel of the mind—the *bodhicitta* in the form of non-emission (*acyuti*), which arises from the union of the thunderbolt and the lotus, and whose innate nature (*sahaja-svabhāva*) is manifest day and night—that supreme lord of yogins knows the reality of the Dharma as it truly is.
No one else does, for others are attached to the pleasure characterized by the friction of the senses. Therefore, it is said:
17. By him who has made a bond for his own mind while it was flowing along its path, the entire triple world was expanded and then withdrawn again.

By that lord of yogins, the *bodhicitta* in the form of vibration (*spanda*) was rendered stable; [thus] the triple world—consisting of the bliss of body and the bliss of mind—[was expanded and reabsorbed]. (157)

The sense is this: having realized one's own nature in its entirety and without remainder as it has manifested, it is then withdrawn and introduced into the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), established within that which is designated as "happiness. Therefore, he says:
"O Goddess, what Tathāgata can be obtained from a multitude of wrathful deities? Abide in the moments of the innate state, free from the circle of the maṇḍala. (18)
This is the meaning:
for what purpose?

The connection is as follows: "In order that the goddess Cittavajra-tathāgata may be found within the host of wrathful deities, I shall abide in the moment of the innate (*sahaja*) at the time of liberation from the mandala-circle."

If the deities of the mandalas of time, body, speech, and mind—beginning with the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—have attained the state of being of one flavor (*samarasībhāva*) through the instruction on great bliss (*mahāsukha*), then this alone is the great mandala; therefore, there is no other separate mandala apart from it.
And so it is said in the *Guṭikātantra*:
"It transcends the meditation on all limbs and is devoid of conceptual construction and its objects."
"Endowed with the measure and the drop, this is the supreme maṇḍala. Thus it is said:

"O King of the Mind, he by whom the mind has been made motionless in the innate state through the state of equal flavor (samarasa) becomes perfected at that very moment; neither old age nor death shall affect him. (19)
This is the meaning:

the connection is that by whichever yogin the *bodhicitta*—which has the nature of being unmoving and unswerving through the means of innate great bliss (*sahaja-mahāsukha*), and which has become a single flavor with the joys of the body (*kāyānanda*) and so forth—is made into the fourth [joy] of the joy of gnosis (*jñānānanda*).
By means of the culmination of that practice, through the arrival of its activity, one becomes an adept (*siddha*), having abandoned old age and death at that very moment.
The meaning is that one performs the *mahāmudrā*.
And so it is said in the *Śrīsamāja*: "At the time of the rising of the sun, they attain accomplishment; there is no doubt in this.
Clarifying that very point, he says:
Immovable, free from conceptualization, and free from fluctuation; devoid of rising and setting, and of pure essence—this is what is called Nirvāṇa. (158)
"Wherein the mind performs no action whatsoever.

(20) This is the meaning: it is "immovable" because it is not shaken by the winds of all conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*); it is "free from discursive thought" (*nirvikalpa*) because it is devoid of agitation; it is "unchanging" because it transcends the senses; and it is "reaching the limit of arising" because it is free from coming and going, resembling the cloudless midday of autumn.
This Nirvāṇa is said to have its own intrinsic form;
therein, whatever mind or consciousness there may be, and the eighty-four classes of mental formations, perform no action whatsoever.
In such a state, not even the slightest conceptualization of self, other, or both arises.
In this context, the meaning is "the moment of the arising of luminous gnosis.
One who awakens to the syllable *Evaṃ* awakens to everything without exception;
he is indeed the casket of the Dharma, wearing the garb of his own Lord. 21.
This is the meaning:

regarding the term "evam" (thus), it refers to the Mahāmudrā, whose nature is the inseparability of emptiness and compassion. By that lord of yogins through whom this "evam" is realized, the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth, are likewise realized.
That very Mahāmudrā, in the form of the casket of Dharma (*dharmakaraṇḍaka*), [arises] from the Dharmakāya.

Therefore, she alone is the essence, the awakening, the attire, the ornament, the decoration, and the splendor—meaning the beautiful adornment—of their casket-necks, namely of their own Lord Vajradhara.
And so it is said in the *Śrī Hevajra*:
That which has the form of the letter *E*, divine, adorned in its center with the syllable *Vaṃ*,
is the abode of all happiness, the jewel-casket of the Buddhas.
It is also stated elsewhere:
The letter *e* is the Mother, while the letter *va* is the Lord of Passion (*ratādhipa*).
The bindu is the Unstruck Knowledge (*anāhata-jñāna*), and from it all other letters are born.
(159) If one sees at the gateway of the movement of the wind, then the drum-beat (*tāla*) is also granted.
If one’s mind becomes steady even in that terrible darkness, and if that jewel within the belly touches the sky, Kṛṣṇa says: while experiencing worldly existence, even nirvāṇa is accomplished. 22.
This is the meaning:

the gateway for the movement of the wind is there; in that place, this which is called "the indivisible" (*abhedya*)—the sealing together of the two halves—is applied to block the paths of the moon and the sun.

If, within that terrible darkness, the activity of the mind (*manovṛtti*), which is the *bodhicitta*, is made into a lamp because it illuminates great bliss (*mahāsukha*), then that jewel of the Victor (*jinaratna*) is the *avadhūtī*, known as the supreme sky (*varagagaṇa*), the lotus situated above and below.
He touches him and embraces him.
To the question "What would happen by this?", he says:
Kṛṣṇavajra declares that when existence is thus experienced—while one is undergoing the enjoyment of the five qualities of sensual pleasure—nirvāṇa, the state of Mahāmudrā, becomes manifest.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"He who has truly made the mind motionless perceives the syllable of Dharma;
at that moment, the winds are bound and the poisons become powerless. (23)
This is the meaning:

that person, having rendered the mind—the *bodhicitta*—immobile through the union of the vajra and the lotus, also binds the wind, the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), to the side of the *mahāmudrā*, the unstruck syllable (*anāhatākṣara*) characterized as previously described;
the meaning is that at that very moment, no other interval is required.
Because it is free from the transformations of the eighteen elements.
And so Saraha-pāda said:
"Those elements have become utterly diminished, since this very wind is independent."
That passionate woman, clinging to the neck of her lover, even now asks: "Is this bodily pleasure my friend?
Surely that syllable of Dharma—where is it to be found? (160) Thus she utters the supreme *paramavirama* [juncture].
In the midst of those syllables of the Dharma, one perceives the mark;
if this sign is clearly realized, then the wife of the wind is bound motionless there. 24.
This is the meaning:
disregard both supreme cessation (*paramavirama*) and passion-cessation (*rāgavirāga*), which consist of the forms of *kāla* and *vikāla*.
Therein, one should perceive in the center the syllable of Dharma, characterized as previously described, in the form of the sixteenth digit (*ṣoḍaśīkalā*).

In order to demonstrate the instruction on the previously mentioned *jñānamudrā*, he says: if this *jñānamudrā* is clearly accomplished—that is, brought to perfection—by such an instruction of the *mantranaya*, then what happens? He says:
the "housewife" (*gṛhiṇī*), namely that *jñānamudrā* who has the form of a corpse (*śavarī*), is firmly constrained; the meaning is that she becomes motionless.

Now, while the female Śabara has indeed fallen, what is the state of the male Śabara and where does he dwell? To this he says: On the lofty peak of the excellent mountain, where the sages and Śabaras have made their dwelling, that place cannot be traversed even by lions; it is difficult to reach for even the best of elephants. (25)

That very Varagiri—meaning that same peak or summit in the location of the mountain previously mentioned—is "lofty" (*uttuṅga*) because it is the support of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Therein was made the dwelling by the Blessed One, the Śavara Vajradhara.

To the question of what kind [of dwelling] it was, he says: "It is not transgressed nor stepped upon by anyone. This refers to the elephant-king of the mind, which is like a noble elephant of the vital winds (*prāṇapavana*) consisting of the five mandalas; [the dwelling is] "farther away" from that.
This is that supreme mountain described by me; this is that state of great bliss.
For as long as one obtains even a single moment of innate bliss during the night, [that is it]. 26.
(161) This is the meaning.

That very best of mountains has been described by me as the "Black Thunderbolt" (kṛṣṇavajra) and not by anyone else; others like me are not capable of describing it. By way of exposition, this very place of great bliss (mahāsukha) is the aforementioned plateau (sthalī).
Therefore, realize that very state of Nirvāṇa characterized by great bliss, until one attains the station of the Vajradhara who is the lord of the fourteen stages.

Anticipating the question, "What kind of one is this Vajradhara?", he says: The entire world—body, speech, and mind—shines forth as unified; yet that very same [world] shines forth in such a way that it is far away.
This very thing, when broken down, is the Great Bliss, the unique Nirvāṇa. 27.
This is the meaning:

all those Tathāgatas, Vairocana and the others, are the forms of the world by way of the nature of the five aggregates, beginning with form (*rūpa*). Their body, speech, and mind are in the form of earth and the other elements; when they are united and become one with those goddesses, such as Vairocanī and the others, there arises the state of great passion (*mahārāga*) and so forth, characterized by perfect awakening—the body of the Vajradhara. Through these, there is a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhāva*) according to the analogy of milk and water. Within that very body of Vajradhara, that same [body, speech, and mind] exists according to the analogy of water and its waves.
It flashes forth;
by this, the meaning is that the triple world is the body of Vajradhara.
If one [mantra] is performed, neither mantra nor tantra is needed.
Taking his own wife, he indulges in sport;
as long as one does not sport with one's own wife at home, how can one wander through the five-colored [world]? 28.
This is its meaning:

not even a single mantra is recited, nor is there the chanting of mantras; no tantra is studied, nor is there the recitation of tantras. Having taken one's own wife as the *jñānamudrā*—who appears as pure through the instruction of a true guru—the yogi should remain engaged in amorous play (*keli*) with her.
And he spoke thus:
(162) "Some [images] are merely appearances produced in the mind, resembling the reflection of the moon;
they are to be cultivated by the lords of yogins, those supreme sons of the Conquerors who have been served by the Buddhas."
That flame of gnosis, having increased, burns the entire host of Māra together with its objects;
and through the yoga of the rains, it also burns away passion and the like within the bodies of yogins, along with their equal pleasure.
A yogin who is attached to this Blessed Lady should not engage in the grasping of mantras and tantras.
One's own wife is the form of the Mahāmudrā; therein, she alone is the Jñānamudrā. As long as she does not dissolve or merge [into it], what is accomplished by means of the five-colored forms?
Thus, demonstrating with certainty that the fruit of this very Mahāmudrā is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), he says again:
"This [is for] recitation, fire-offerings, and mandala-rites."
Even if you practice the Dharma day after day,
without the constant love for a young woman,
can enlightenment be attained even with this very body? 29.
"O fool, why do you remain day after day with this external fire-sacrifice (*homa*) and the rites of the mandala? In what manner is your mind so deluded?
How can all of this be fruitless?
Without her—the youthful *Mahāmudrā* who is the very essence of passion—there is no uninterrupted love; without that, how can *Mahāmudrā* be attained by means of this human body?"
Is it true that awakening cannot be attained through another body after discarding the human body?
Why? Because of the statement: "Men are of the form of Vajradhara, and women are Vajrayoṣits. He states the fruit of that [realization]:
"Having awakened to the rare moment of the innate (*sahaja*), one will realize the Vedas and Purāṇas."
"O, the entire world, with its multitude of conceptualizations and objects, is finite!

(30)" The meaning is this: by that yogin who has realized the nature of Mahāmudrā—which is eternally arisen and characterized by the innate (*sahaja*)—the mind, along with all its remaining conceptual constructions and ego-grasping, has been shattered and uprooted from what was previously known through scripture.
Having made his jewel-like mind steady, he takes his own consort here.
O Vajra, listen; I have spoken the ultimate truth.
(31) The meaning is as follows:

By him who has made the jewel of the mind—the *bodhicitta*—immovable because it cannot be shaken by the fierce woman (*pracaṇḍālī*), this very divine consort (*divyamudrā*) is his own wife. In that very place, the *evaṃkāra*, which is the abode of great bliss (*mahāsukha*)...
Thus has this supreme, uncontrived meaning been spoken by me, Kṛṣṇavajra— the Vajrin, the Holder of the Vajra, the Protector, the Lord of body, speech, and mind.
The meaning is that there is nothing else besides this.
Clarifying this very point, he says:
"Just as salt dissolves in water, so too is the mind captivated by a wife; it becomes immortal in an instant, provided that it remains constant toward her. (32)
This is the meaning:

just as salt dissolves in water, so too the housewife, who is the nature of gnosis (*jñāna*), takes hold of the mind and enters into a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) and single integration (*ekalolībhāva*). If at that very moment one remains eternally together with that housewife, who is the nature of the blissful mind, by this the Vajrasattva of the "yoked pair" (*yuganaddha*) is demonstrated.
Thus ends the *Mekhalā-ṭīkā*, a commentary on the *Dohā-kośa* composed by the venerable Ācārya.
